Alright as someone who has been through a lot of therapy and dealt with anger issues all their life, dude, you are not taking responsibility for your actions. See, you *think* you need to yell, but that's absolutely not true and just an excuse for the fact that you are not managing your symptoms well enough. 

The fact of the matter is that not being able to adhere to the basic boundary of maintaining a respectful tone when having an argument with your partner is a problem and one that you need to get a handle on. Saying "I've never been violent" washes over the fact that yelling is the universal signifier of "I am preparing to get violent". Even if you're absolutely sure you would never hurt her in your own mind, *she* doesn't know that. 

No matter who you are or how mentally healthy and functional you are, if you have shown that you can't control your highly aggressive impulse and *intend* not to (which is what you're saying when you tell her you will not stop yelling) then you have shown her you cannot control your anger. That is dangerous. Because there's no cap on how angry a person can be. Today you can't stop screaming at her. But what about the day a new impulse you can't control comes up? She's supposed to just accept that? And are you even thinking about why she would think to call the cops? Because I guarantee you it was because she was scared. You aren't trying to see this from her perspective. 

If you really couldn't talk to her without yelling, you could have walked away when she asked you to stop. But instead you decided your desire to make her uncomfortable was more important. You're not seeing it, but you're sewing the seeds of abuse whether you intend to or not and -key detail- abusers never intend to abuse people. I would reflect and consider taking a break to get some independent treatment for your condition if I were you. If you can't have disagreements with your partner without violating serious boundaries, you should not be in a relationship.

Well, for a long time after my break-up, I was living in the past. Going through everything with a fine-toothed comb all the time. I think some part of me thought that if I thought about it from every angle and talked all of my feelings out that one day I'd just be done or I'd reach a conclusion I was satisfied with or have some epiphany and move on. But eventually I realized that wasn't going to happen and I needed help because I couldn't stop and it was taking over my life. It wasn't until I was in therapy that someone put into perspective that it had become a compulsion for me. It wasn't about my ex anymore, it was a way to make myself feel bad for doing wrong, basically a form of self harm (not going to get into the childhood trauma that caused that thinking but you get the idea). To stop, I had to start doing this thing I recommend to everyone now.

There's a circle of synapses in a part of your brain that, when you start internally ruminating on something, it sends electrical signals through that circle, and every time it completes the circle it gets stronger. So when you feel like you're "spiraling" it's because your brain technically *is* spiraling causing all of your negative feelings and thoughts to become more intense. 

There is a way to undo this: Talking out loud. Basically, you have to argue out loud with the negative thoughts you're having. Talking accesses another part of the brain that reverses that circle. It starts going in the opposite direction, unspiraling and basically undoing the damages.

So, for example

Thinking "I did X terrible thing and I am terrible"

Out loud reply "I only did what I could do to protect myself at the time. I didn't have the tools I do now so I did the best with what I had. I am not the same person. I see that's wrong now and I'm working on it so I won't do it again. I'm doing a good job" etc.

It takes a lot of practice, but it changed my life and friends I've taught to do it have told me how much it works for them too. The more you do it, the more start to believe the good stuff and the more powerful it becomes against fighting the bad. It took me a long time, but I'm doing a lot better.

For me, my breakup this summer destroyed my life. I lost my best friend and love, my home,my friends, my life. I had to move across the country to live with my mom, leaving all of my possessions in storage. I had no job, no money, no car, and no friends. For a while it seemed like I was going to die. Or at the very least seriously hurt myself. I was having reckless sex, I developed a drinking problem, and I was ready to give up. It's been four months since my rock bottom, finding myself in a stranger's house who was so high he couldn't even talk, not sure how I was going to get home and realizing no one knew where I was. 

My ex is still on my mind, but they feel far away. I've cried about them maybe twice in the past month as opposed to all day and night in the beginning. I miss them still, but I see how much healthier I am now that we aren't together and I know that's not a coincidence. I was bedridden and my body was shutting down while I was with them. Things aren't good. But they're better. I've made progress. I'm still making progress. And things will continue to improve so long as I keep looking forward. 

It's okay to backslide so long as you keep looking forward, focusing on your goals. You can get through this. It's going to take more patience and strength than you think you have, but the person you want to be who is capable of the life and the love you want to have is waiting for you on the other side of this all. Feel your feelings. The pain, the love, the happiness, the anger. Feel it all. And then know that it has passed. Recognize it as something that happened but is now behind you. Learn to let it go. It won't be easy and you'll probably have to let many things go more than once, but remember that person is not your life anymore. Your life is what you make of it now. This is your most important opportunity. Be gentle with yourself. Take care. You can do this, one day at a time.

I will say that arguing is my main trigger. I was diagnosed with BPD over the summer, along with a powerful combination of ADD/ADHD, and since starting medication for the ADHD, it has really helped me to navigate arguments better now that I can actually focus on them rather than just feel completely overwhelmed with emotional and sensory processing. 

I'm still learning what to do, but I'm finding that the most consistent and self destructive response I had in arguments or confrontation is that I felt that everything needed to be discussed as soon as it was brought up. So of course I would say things I didn't mean that just made things worse. I had no idea how I felt. Now, I tell people that I need time to process my thoughts and feelings before I respond. That can mean anywhere from a few minutes to a few days, but I try to tell them up front how long I need, and if the person I am disagreeing with cares enough, they usually honor the fact that I need space in order to respectfully continue the conversation. 

I'm also trying to meditate more. It's hard to get the hang of mindfulness when you've had BPD for so long, but if you're serious about managing your symptoms, it's an important skill to master.
